Mecanum Chassis Guide

Prolabs Robotics. A goBILDA style FTC chassis with 4 x 104 mm mecanum wheels and 312 RPM Yellow Jacket motors. Build, wiring, configuration, code and testing.
Mecanum chassis, front right
Top view: rollers make an X
Rollers must make an X when you look from above. If you see an O, two wheels are swapped.
Created by: Aarav J.
Collaborators: R-Factor FRC

5 build steps, then wiring, configuration, code, a first drive test and troubleshooting.
Costs are approximate. Nothing in this guide has been tested on our robot yet unless we say so.

Before you start

In the picturesMeaning
Dark part: the part you add or move in this step
Light grey part: already on the robot
Black arrow: move the part this way

What this guide is. A simple, goBILDA style mecanum chassis: a U-channel frame, 4 direct drive motors, and 4 mecanum wheels held by the motor shaft on one side and a bearing on the other. It is one good way to build it, not the only way. If you want everything in one box, the goBILDA Strafer Chassis Kit is a complete, tested alternative (see the parts list).

Directions. Front is the side marked FRONT in the pictures. Left and right are as seen from behind the robot, looking forward. All sizes are in mm.

3D printed parts. This chassis does not need printed parts. If you print any extra parts (wire guides, covers, mounts), print them at 100% infill.

More reading. The Mecanum Wheels Presentation in this same folder explains how mecanum wheels move, with the maths. Our Shooter Trajectory Calculations doc (FTC Docs folder) uses the robot position this chassis gives you.

How fast will it go?

Wheel circumference = pi x 104 mm = about 327 mm. At 312 RPM (no load), that is 312 / 60 x 0.327 m = about 1.70 m/s (about 5.57 ft/s) forward, in theory. goBILDA lists the same 5.57 ft/s for the Strafer kit. Real speed is lower because of load and battery voltage, and strafing sideways is slower than driving forward.

Mecanum Chassis Guide | Page 3 of 15

The roller pattern: X is right, O is wrong

Look straight down on the robot. The top rollers of all four wheels should point towards the centre of the robot, like the two lines of an X.

Each mecanum wheel has rollers at 45 degrees. A set has two kinds of wheels, often called left and right. The front left and back right wheels are one kind, and the front right and back left wheels are the other kind. gm0 explains that a standard mecanum drive has the wheels in an X shape, with the rollers angled towards the centre when you look from above.

The O mistake. If two wheels are swapped, the rollers make an O. The robot still drives forward, backward and turns, so the mistake is easy to miss. But when you try to strafe, it moves badly or turns on the spot instead. Always do the strafe test in the first drive checklist.

Our 3D model, from above (X)
Same robot with wheels swapped (O)

In the bottom rollers (the ones touching the mat), the pattern looks the other way round. That is normal. Always check from above.

1aLay out the two side railsStep 1 of 5: Build the frame
Put the two 384 mm U-channels on a flat table, open side up, parallel to each other.
Parts2 x 1120 Series U-Channel, 15 hole, 384 mm
Size and positionOutside to outside, the frame is 288 mm + 2 x 48 mm = 384 mm wide, so the frame is about 384 x 384 mm.
TipBuild on a flat table. A frame built on an uneven floor can twist, and then one wheel lifts off the mat.
1bAdd the cross channels and check squareStep 1 of 5: Build the frame
Fit the two 288 mm U-channels between the side rails, one at the front and one at the back. Screw them in loosely, then measure both diagonals.
Parts2 x 1120 Series U-Channel, 11 hole, 288 mm, corner brackets or plates, M4 screws
Size and positionThe two diagonals must be the same length, within about 1 mm. Then tighten every screw.
TipIf the diagonals differ, push the long diagonal corners together a little, then measure again.
Mecanum Chassis Guide | Page 5 of 15
2aMount the four motorsStep 2 of 5: Motors
Bolt one 312 RPM Yellow Jacket motor at each corner, with the 8 mm REX output shaft pointing out through the side rail.
Parts4 x 5203 Series Yellow Jacket, 19.2:1, 312 RPM, motor mounts, M4 screws
Size and positionAll four shafts at the same height. Front and back shafts at the same distance from the frame ends.
TipMark each motor FL, FR, BL and BR with tape now. It saves a lot of time when wiring.
Close-up: shaft through the side rail
2bCheck the shaft lines from aboveStep 2 of 5: Motors
Look down on the frame. The left and right shafts at the front must be on one straight line. Do the same for the back.
Size and positionFront pair on one line, back pair on one line, and the two lines parallel.
TipA motor that is a little crooked makes the robot drift and wobble. Fix it now, before the wheels go on.
Mecanum Chassis Guide | Page 6 of 15
3aAdd spacers and the outer bearingStep 3 of 5: Bearings, spacers and wheels
Fit spacers (standoffs) from the side rail, and an outer plate with a bearing, so the wheel shaft is held on both sides of the wheel.
PartsSpacers, 1 outer plate per wheel, 1 bearing per wheel, M4 screws
Size and positionLeave a small gap (about 1 to 2 mm) between the wheel and the rail, and between the wheel and the outer plate.
Which wayThe bearing sits on the same line as the motor shaft.
TipA wheel held only by the motor shaft can bend the shaft when the robot is hit. The outer bearing stops this.
3bFit the four wheelsStep 3 of 5: Bearings, spacers and wheels
Put each wheel on its shaft with a hub. The GripForce set has 2 left wheels and 2 right wheels. Put them on so the rollers make an X when you look from above (see page 5).
Parts1 x GripForce Mecanum Wheel Set, 104 mm (4 wheels), 4 hubs
Size and positionFront left and back right are the same type. Front right and back left are the other type.
TipCheck the X before you tighten the hubs. Swapping two wheels later is slow.
Close-up: wheel between the rail and the outer plate
Mecanum Chassis Guide | Page 7 of 15
4aCheck the X from aboveStep 4 of 5: Check and balance
Look straight down on the robot. The top rollers of the four wheels must point towards the centre, making an X.
Size and positionFront left rollers: top left to bottom right. Front right: top right to bottom left. Back wheels: the mirror.
Which wayIf you see an O (rollers going round the robot), two wheels are swapped. See page 5.
TipTake a photo from above and draw the lines on it. It makes the X easy to see.
4bPlace the hub and battery low and centralStep 4 of 5: Check and balance
Mount the Control Hub and the battery inside the frame, low down and near the centre.
Size and positionTry to keep the centre of mass near the middle of the four wheels. Heavy parts low.
Which wayKeep the USB and ports of the Control Hub easy to reach.
TipIf one corner is much lighter, that wheel slips and the robot drifts when strafing.

Step 5a: Wire the motors to the Control Hub

MotorControl Hub motor portEncoder portConfiguration name
Front left (FL)00frontLeftMotor
Back left (BL)11backLeftMotor
Front right (FR)22frontRightMotor
Back right (BR)33backRightMotor
Built-in IMUinside the hubimu (added by default)

The port numbers are our choice. Any order works, as long as the names in the configuration match the code. The names above are the same as the gm0 sample code, so you can use that code without changes.

  • The motor power cable goes into the motor port. The encoder cable goes into the encoder port with the same number. If they do not match, the encoder reads the wrong motor.
  • Battery to the power switch, power switch to the Control Hub. Mount the switch where the referee can reach it.
  • Zip tie every cable to the frame, away from the wheels. A cable caught in a mecanum roller can rip out a connector.
  • Pull gently on every connector before each match. Loose cables are the most common reason a robot stops in a match.
Mecanum Chassis Guide | Page 9 of 15

Step 5b: Make the robot configuration

  1. On the Driver Hub, tap the 3 dots menu, then Configure Robot, then New.
  2. Tap Control Hub Portal, then Control Hub, then Motors.
  3. For ports 0 to 3, choose the motor type goBILDA 5202/3/4 series and type the names from the table on the last page. Names are case sensitive: frontLeftMotor is not the same as FrontLeftMotor.
  4. Check that the IMU is listed as imu (under I2C bus 0). It is added by default on a new configuration.
  5. Tap Done, then Save. Give the configuration a name (for example mecanum) and activate it. The robot restarts.

These steps follow the FTC Docs page Creating a Configuration (see Sources). If the code says it cannot find a device, the name in the configuration and the name in the code do not match.

Step 6: Set the motor directions

gm0 notes that most FTC motors spin counterclockwise (seen from the shaft end) when given positive power. On a direct drive chassis like ours, the motors on the two sides face opposite ways, so one side must be reversed in code. The gm0 sample reverses the right side. We start the same way:

frontRightMotor.setDirection(DcMotorSimple.Direction.REVERSE);
backRightMotor.setDirection(DcMotorSimple.Direction.REVERSE);

Test each wheel on its own before you drive. Put the robot on a box so the wheels are off the ground. Then give each motor a small positive power, one at a time:

// Test OpMode idea: hold a button to spin one motor forward slowly
if (gamepad1.x) frontLeftMotor.setPower(0.3);   // X = front left
if (gamepad1.y) frontRightMotor.setPower(0.3);  // Y = front right
if (gamepad1.a) backLeftMotor.setPower(0.3);    // A = back left
if (gamepad1.b) backRightMotor.setPower(0.3);   // B = back right
What you seeWhat to do
Every wheel spins so the robot would move forwardGood. Go to the code
All four spin backwardReverse the left side instead of the right
One wheel spins the wrong wayReverse only that motor in code, or check it is in the right port
The wrong wheel spinsThe cable is in the wrong port, or the names are swapped in the configuration

Step 7a: Robot-centric drive code (Java)

Left stick moves the robot (forward, back, sideways, any angle). Right stick turns it. "Forward" on the stick is always the front of the robot. This is the gm0 sample, with our comments.

package org.firstinspires.ftc.teamcode;

import com.qualcomm.robotcore.eventloop.opmode.LinearOpMode;
import com.qualcomm.robotcore.eventloop.opmode.TeleOp;
import com.qualcomm.robotcore.hardware.DcMotor;
import com.qualcomm.robotcore.hardware.DcMotorSimple;

// Robot-centric mecanum drive. Based on the gm0 "Mecanum TeleOp" sample.
@TeleOp
public class MecanumTeleOp extends LinearOpMode {
    @Override
    public void runOpMode() throws InterruptedException {
        // Names must match the robot configuration
        DcMotor frontLeftMotor = hardwareMap.dcMotor.get("frontLeftMotor");
        DcMotor backLeftMotor = hardwareMap.dcMotor.get("backLeftMotor");
        DcMotor frontRightMotor = hardwareMap.dcMotor.get("frontRightMotor");
        DcMotor backRightMotor = hardwareMap.dcMotor.get("backRightMotor");

        // Reverse the right side. If the robot drives backward, reverse the left side instead.
        frontRightMotor.setDirection(DcMotorSimple.Direction.REVERSE);
        backRightMotor.setDirection(DcMotorSimple.Direction.REVERSE);

        waitForStart();
        if (isStopRequested()) return;

        while (opModeIsActive()) {
            double y = -gamepad1.left_stick_y;      // Y stick is reversed
            double x = gamepad1.left_stick_x * 1.1; // 1.1 counteracts imperfect strafing
            double rx = gamepad1.right_stick_x;     // turning

            // Normalise: divide by the largest total so every power stays in [-1, 1]
            // and the ratio between the wheels is kept.
            double denominator = Math.max(Math.abs(y) + Math.abs(x) + Math.abs(rx), 1);
            double frontLeftPower = (y + x + rx) / denominator;
            double backLeftPower = (y - x + rx) / denominator;
            double frontRightPower = (y - x - rx) / denominator;
            double backRightPower = (y + x - rx) / denominator;

            frontLeftMotor.setPower(frontLeftPower);
            backLeftMotor.setPower(backLeftPower);
            frontRightMotor.setPower(frontRightPower);
            backRightMotor.setPower(backRightPower);
        }
    }
}

The 1.1 strafe factor. Mecanum wheels strafe a little slower than they drive forward, because of roller friction. Multiplying x by 1.1 makes sideways and diagonal driving feel more even. gm0 uses 1.1, but it is up to your driver: try 1.0 to 1.2.

Step 7b: Field-centric drive code (Java)

With field-centric drive, pushing the stick forward always moves the robot away from the driver, whichever way the robot is facing. It uses the IMU inside the Control Hub. Press OPTIONS (START on Xbox style gamepads) to reset forward.

package org.firstinspires.ftc.teamcode;

import com.qualcomm.hardware.rev.RevHubOrientationOnRobot;
import com.qualcomm.robotcore.eventloop.opmode.LinearOpMode;
import com.qualcomm.robotcore.eventloop.opmode.TeleOp;
import com.qualcomm.robotcore.hardware.DcMotor;
import com.qualcomm.robotcore.hardware.DcMotorSimple;
import com.qualcomm.robotcore.hardware.IMU;
import org.firstinspires.ftc.robotcore.external.navigation.AngleUnit;

// Field-centric mecanum drive. Based on the gm0 "Field-Centric Final Sample Code".
@TeleOp
public class FieldCentricMecanumTeleOp extends LinearOpMode {
    @Override
    public void runOpMode() throws InterruptedException {
        DcMotor frontLeftMotor = hardwareMap.dcMotor.get("frontLeftMotor");
        DcMotor backLeftMotor = hardwareMap.dcMotor.get("backLeftMotor");
        DcMotor frontRightMotor = hardwareMap.dcMotor.get("frontRightMotor");
        DcMotor backRightMotor = hardwareMap.dcMotor.get("backRightMotor");
        frontRightMotor.setDirection(DcMotorSimple.Direction.REVERSE);
        backRightMotor.setDirection(DcMotorSimple.Direction.REVERSE);

        IMU imu = hardwareMap.get(IMU.class, "imu");
        // Change these two to match how YOUR Control Hub is mounted
        IMU.Parameters parameters = new IMU.Parameters(new RevHubOrientationOnRobot(
                RevHubOrientationOnRobot.LogoFacingDirection.UP,
                RevHubOrientationOnRobot.UsbFacingDirection.FORWARD));
        imu.initialize(parameters);

        waitForStart();
        if (isStopRequested()) return;

        while (opModeIsActive()) {
            double y = -gamepad1.left_stick_y;
            double x = gamepad1.left_stick_x;
            double rx = gamepad1.right_stick_x;

            if (gamepad1.options) {   // reset "forward" to where the robot faces now
                imu.resetYaw();
            }
            double botHeading = imu.getRobotYawPitchRollAngles().getYaw(AngleUnit.RADIANS);

            // Rotate the joystick direction against the robot heading
            double rotX = x * Math.cos(-botHeading) - y * Math.sin(-botHeading);
            double rotY = x * Math.sin(-botHeading) + y * Math.cos(-botHeading);
            rotX = rotX * 1.1;  // counteract imperfect strafing

            double denominator = Math.max(Math.abs(rotY) + Math.abs(rotX) + Math.abs(rx), 1);
            frontLeftMotor.setPower((rotY + rotX + rx) / denominator);
            backLeftMotor.setPower((rotY - rotX + rx) / denominator);
            frontRightMotor.setPower((rotY - rotX - rx) / denominator);
            backRightMotor.setPower((rotY + rotX - rx) / denominator);
        }
    }
}

Normalising. The SDK clips any power above 1 to 1. Without the denominator, powers like 0.4, 0.1, 1.1 and 1.4 would become 0.4, 0.1, 1.0 and 1.0, and the robot would curve. Dividing all four by the largest total keeps the same ratio (gm0).

Step 8: First drive test checklist

Do these in order, at low speed first, on a clear floor or field tiles. One person drives, one person holds the power switch.

Battery charged, power switch easy to reach, every cable zip tied away from the wheels
Robot on a box: each wheel spins forward on its own (step 6)
Rollers make an X from above (page 5)
Left stick forward: robot drives straight forward
Left stick back: robot drives straight back
Left stick right: robot strafes right without turning much
Left stick left: robot strafes left without turning much
Left stick diagonal: robot moves at about 45 degrees
Right stick: robot turns on the spot, both ways
Drive forward and turn at the same time: smooth curve, no jerks
Full speed for 2 tile lengths: robot stays straight, no wobble or noise
Field-centric only: turn the robot 90 degrees, push forward, robot still moves away from you
After 5 minutes of driving: check every screw, hub and wheel for looseness
If the robot turns when you ask it to strafe, check the X pattern first, then the motor directions, then the weight balance.

Troubleshooting

ProblemWhat to check, and the fix
It drifts or turns when strafingCheck the X pattern from above. Check every wheel spins the right way. Move heavy parts so the weight is even on all 4 wheels. Check all 4 wheels touch the mat (a twisted frame lifts one). Try a strafe factor between 1.0 and 1.2. For autonomous, use the IMU to hold the heading.
A wheel spins the wrong wayReverse that motor with setDirection in code, or check that the motor cable is in the right port and the names in the configuration are not swapped.
The wrong wheel spinsThe motor is in a different port from the one in the configuration. Move the cable or fix the name.
Wobble or shaking at speedA hub or set screw is loose, a wheel is not straight on its shaft, a roller is damaged or has dirt in it, or a shaft is bent. Check the outer bearing is fitted and in line.
Robot is heavy on one side or the frontMove the battery and the Control Hub towards the centre, low down. A light corner slips and drifts. Weigh each corner with a kitchen scale if you can.
Robot curves when driving forwardA motor is weaker or a wheel is dragging. Spin each wheel by hand to feel for rubbing. Check the frame is square (step 1b).
Robot does nothing, or the code crashes on INITNames in the code and the configuration do not match (case sensitive), or the configuration is not active.
Field-centric goes the wrong wayThe IMU orientation (logo and USB direction) does not match how the hub is mounted, or you did not reset the yaw facing forward.
Strafing is very slowThis is normal for mecanum, a little. If very slow, check the X pattern and the strafe factor.

Common mistakes

Wheels in an O pattern instead of an X
Encoder cable in a different port number from its motor
Frame not square, so one wheel lifts off the mat
Wheel held only by the motor shaft, with no outer bearing, on a heavy robot
Cables near the wheels, where a roller can catch them
Heavy parts all on one side or high up
Forgetting to normalise the powers, so the robot curves at full stick
